tour.title: Baku: Old City to the Caspian
tour.summary: Eight centuries in under three kilometres of walking — walled khans' palaces, Silk Road caravanserais, a funicular ride, and sunset over the Caspian.
tour.overviewText:
Baku hits you first as wind. It shoves down the boulevard, rattles the café umbrellas and carries a faint mineral tang off the Caspian — Baku's name may even come from an old Persian phrase for windswept. Then you notice the second thing: money. Glass towers shaped like flames, a carpet museum shaped like a rolled carpet, a waterfront that gleams after dark. This is a city that got rich fast and decided to look like it.

Why Baku matters starts a mile underground. This peninsula leaks oil and gas — flames burst from the rock, and medieval travellers wrote about fire-worshippers praying at natural vents. In the late 19th century that geology made Baku the oil capital of the world, built by Swedish Nobels and French Rothschilds, worked by Azerbaijani, Russian, Armenian and Persian labourers side by side. Fortunes paved the mansions you still see downtown. Then the Soviets took the fields, industrialised them ruthlessly, and left behind boulevards, institutes and pollution in equal measure. Independent Azerbaijan since 1991 has ridden a second oil boom, and the skyline you see is what that boom bought.

To understand the streets you walk, hold three facts together. First, Azerbaijan is a secular Muslim-majority country — most people identify as Muslim but practise privately, and mosques share the Old City with synagogues, churches and a fire-temple memory. Second, Karabakh — the mountainous region contested between Armenia and Azerbaijan in wars in the 1990s, retaken by Azerbaijan in the 2020 war and the 2023 offensive, after which around 100,000 Armenians fled — is a live grief here, and you will stand at its memorial on this walk. Third, the country has been governed by one family since 1993, father then son; supporters credit stability and rebuilding, critics point to constrained elections and press freedoms. You do not need to pick a side to walk honestly — just know the argument exists.

The walk itself is simple. You start inside the walled Old City among 12th- and 15th-century stone, ride the little funicular railway up the steep hill, and finish down on the Caspian promenade as the Flame Towers switch on. Under three kilometres of walking covers eight centuries.

Practicals, plainly. The route is about 5.2 km and 80 minutes of actual walking, easy to moderate: flat cobbled lanes in the Old City, then a gentle downhill from the hilltop to the sea. The steep climb is ridden, not walked — the funicular costs about 1 manat each way. The manat, code AZN, is the local currency; museum tickets on this route run around 10 to 15 manat, the small museums are free, and every fee and hour in this guide is approximate, so verify at the gate and carry small notes. A caravanserai, by the way — you will visit one — is a fortified Silk Road inn where camel caravans slept and traded, and a funicular is a small cable-hauled car that climbs a slope on rails. Start early afternoon, around 1 to 2pm, so the museums are open and you reach the hilltop for the golden hour before sunset. Wear shoes that forgive cobbles, carry water and a head covering for the mosque, and keep your voice low at the memorial.

Come for the flames — natural, Soviet and LED. Stay for the small things: the inscription on a minaret, the tiniest book you will ever see, the names on the graves. Baku rewards walkers who look closely.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Flat cobbled lanes in the Old City, the steep hill is ridden via funicular, then a gentle downhill walk to the boulevard. The Maiden Tower's internal stairs are steep and narrow; the Old City underfoot is cobbles and worn stone.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start early afternoon, around 1 to 2pm, so the museums are open and you reach the hilltop for late golden light. Time the viewpoint for the hour before sunset, and finish on the boulevard as the Flame Towers switch on their LED flames after dark. Mornings work too, but the light over the bay is an evening show.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Maiden Tower
stops.narration:
Stop here and look up. This is the Maiden Tower — Qiz Qalasi in Azerbaijani, which means exactly the same thing — and it is the oldest and strangest thing in Baku. The stone cylinder in front of you went up in the 12th century, eight floors of pale limestone with walls five metres thick at the base. Climb it in a minute. First, understand the riddle, because the riddle is the point.

Nobody knows what it was for. Fortress? Too awkward to defend, with its odd projecting fin. Fire temple? Possibly — this peninsula had natural gas flames bursting from the rock, and the ancient Persian religion of Zoroastrianism, which prayed to fire, was strong here. Observatory? Some windows catch the sun on particular alignments. Every theory has a professor behind it and a hole in it. Any guide who tells you otherwise is improvising.

The legend every local child learns is darker. A khan — a Turco-Mongol title for a ruler, used by Baku's medieval kings — demanded his own daughter in marriage. She stalled him by asking for this tower first, then threw herself from the top into the sea rather than marry him. It almost certainly never happened, but it tells you how Baku sees the tower: defiance cast in stone.

And the sea detail is real. The Caspian once lapped this rock, and ships tied up where cafés now stand; the sea level has risen and fallen by metres over the centuries, so the shoreline walked away from the tower. The museum ticket is around 15 manat — the manat, code AZN, is Azerbaijan's currency — but verify at the gate, and expect roughly 10:00 to 18:00 daily with the ticket office closing an hour early. Inside is steep narrow stairs; climb slowly, watch where 12th-century builders joined older stonework, then walk sixty metres north to the carved portal of the caravanserai.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Museum ticket around 15 ₼, roughly. Prices move and foreign-visitor pricing can differ, so verify at the gate and carry small manat notes.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 10:00 to 18:00, sometimes longer in summer. Ticket office usually closes an hour before the tower. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: steep narrow stone stairs between all eight floors, low doorways, uneven steps. The plaza around the base is level cobbles.
stops.insiderTip: Climb slowly and look at the masonry as you go — you can see where the 12th-century builders joined older stonework. At the top, find the sea-facing fin: that strange rib is the tower's great unsolved mystery.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the tower plaza and walk about sixty metres north up the lane, into the small stone courtyard with the big carved portal. That is the Bukhara Caravanserai, our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bukhara Caravanserai
stops.narration:
Step through that carved portal into a Silk Road truck stop. A caravanserai — the word means a caravan palace, a fortified inn where camel caravans slept, stabled animals, traded and hired guards — and this one was built in the 15th century by merchants from Bukhara, the great trading city in what is now Uzbekistan. Baku was their western terminus: silk and spice came overland from Central Asia and loaded onto ships here across the Caspian.

Read the plan like a business model in stone. One narrow guarded entrance, easy to bar at night. A square courtyard for unloading camels. Two floors of small cells: animals and goods below, merchants above. The stone is pale Absheron limestone, and the carved frame over the portal, with its honeycomb muqarnas stonework — the stepped, stalactite-like carving Islamic masons use to turn corners into curves — is the finest original detail. Everyone photographs the courtyard; look at the doorway instead.

The fact that reframes it: Bukhara merchants did not just pass through, they settled, with their own quarter, mosque and weights and measures, while Baku's khans taxed every bale. This little square made the city's fortune centuries before oil, and sea captains and camel drivers eating in the same courtyard invented a kind of cosmopolitanism before the word existed.

Today it runs as a restaurant, so the courtyard is free to wander but tea is at menu prices. If the portal is shut, admire the stonework from the lane. Then leave, turn left and walk about two hundred metres south-west downhill toward the minaret over the rooftops. The lanes are crooked on purpose — they break the Caspian wind — so follow the minaret, not your sense of direction.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to wander the courtyard. It operates as a restaurant, so food and tea are at menu prices.
stops.openingHours: Courtyard generally accessible through the day and evening with the restaurant. If the portal is shut, admire the carved stonework from the lane.
stops.accessibility: One step through the portal, then a level courtyard. The upper cells are not open to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the portal's carved frame before you go in — the stone muqarnas carving over the door is the building's finest original detail, and everyone photographs the courtyard instead.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard, turn left and walk south-west through the lanes for about two hundred metres, downhill toward the minaret you can see over the rooftops. The Juma Mosque is ahead of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Interfase, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Juma Mosque
stops.narration:
You are standing at Baku's Friday mosque. Juma simply means Friday — the day of the congregational midday prayer, the week's main sermon — and every old Islamic city has one big Juma mosque that works as the community's religious parliament. This is Baku's.

What you see is a layer cake. A mosque has stood here since early Islamic centuries, but wars, earthquakes and Soviet atheism each took a bite. The Soviets closed or demolished mosques across Azerbaijan in the 1930s; this one survived as a museum and carpet workshop, which perversely saved the building by giving it a secular job. The current walls are a 19th-century rebuild on medieval bones, with one genuine survivor: the minaret, dated by its carved inscription band to 1437 in angular Kufic-style script — one of the oldest formal Arabic calligraphy styles, all straight lines and geometry. That inscription is four and a half centuries older than the walls beside it.

Entry is free; this is a working mosque, not a ticketed site, and donations are welcome but never required. The etiquette that matters: shoes off, quiet voices, shoulders and knees covered, women usually offered a headscarf at the door. It stays open daily outside the five prayer times but closes to tourists during prayers and the Friday midday congregation, and prayer times shift daily.

What you learn here is modern Azerbaijan in miniature: a secular state with a Muslim-majority population, where most people believe privately and the mosque fills on Fridays and feast days. Faith survived seventy Soviet years by going quiet, and came back the same way. Leave and walk north-west uphill about two hundred and fifty metres following the palace signs.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a working mosque, not a ticketed site. Donations for upkeep are welcome but never required.
stops.openingHours: Open daily outside the five prayer times. Closed to tourists during prayers and for the Friday midday congregation. Prayer times shift daily.
stops.accessibility: A step or two at the entrance. Shoes are removed inside, so the floor is carpeted and level.
stops.insiderTip: Find the 1437 inscription band on the minaret — Kufic-style carving, easy to miss from the courtyard. It is the oldest dated thing on this stop by four and a half centuries.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque and walk north-west uphill through the lanes for about two hundred and fifty metres, following the signs for the palace complex. The big ceremonial portal ahead is the Palace of the Shirvanshahs.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Palace of the Shirvanshahs
stops.narration:
Climb to this terrace: you are in the seat of a kingdom most visitors never heard of. The Shirvanshahs — the word means the kings, or shahs, of Shirvan, the medieval Muslim state that ruled this coast — moved their court to Baku in the 15th century and built this walled complex: palace, mosque, tomb, bathhouse and ceremonial hall in one enclosure. This is not one building. It is a government in stone.

Walk it like an org chart. The vaulted palace held receptions and the harem. The small mosque served the court. The domed tomb holds the dynasty's dead, carved so finely the limestone looks like lace. The bathhouse sits half-buried, as bathhouses were for insulation, handling hygiene and gossip equally. And the open rotunda with twelve carved columns is the Divankhana — probably a memorial hall or royal council chamber, divan being the council of state. Scholars still argue about its exact use, which puts it in good company with the Maiden Tower down the hill.

The fact that reframes the carving: these kings survived six centuries by paying tribute to whoever was strongest — Mongols, Timurids, Persians, Ottomans — while keeping their own court, coinage and building style. Small-state diplomacy, played brilliantly. Then in 1501 the young Persian shah Ismail took the city, the dynasty faded, and Baku stayed a provincial port until oil made it rich.

The site ticket is around 10 manat; verify at the gate, since rates change and some pavilion is almost always closed for restoration. Expect roughly 10:00 to 18:00 daily, ticket office closing an hour early. Courtyards are cobbled with steps between levels, and the Divankhana photographs best in slanting afternoon light. Then walk fifty metres to the small museum house beside the complex.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Site ticket around 10 ₼, roughly. Verify at the gate — prices and foreign-visitor rates change, and some pavilions occasionally close for restoration.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 10:00 to 18:00. Ticket office usually closes an hour early. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Mixed: courtyards are cobbled with steps between levels, and several pavilions have stairs. The main courtyard is manageable; the full circuit is not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: The Divankhana rotunda photographs best in slanting afternoon light, when the carving throws deep shadows. And ask the attendants which pavilion is closed — there is almost always one, and it is never the one you expected.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the palace complex and walk about fifty metres to the small museum house beside it — the Museum of Miniature Books, our next stop, is right next door.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Museum of Miniature Books
stops.narration:
This tiny house beside the palace holds one of the strangest museums you will ever enter. The Museum of Miniature Books is exactly that: thousands of tiny books, some smaller than a postage stamp, in glass cases across two or three cramped rooms. Entry is free, by the founder's principle — and the founder is real, Zarifa Salakhova, a Baku collector who spent decades assembling one of the world's largest private collections of miniature books and gave it a public home. Private obsession, public gift.

Ask for a magnifying glass, because you will need it. The collection spans more than seventy countries: thumb-sized Pushkin, a miniature Quran you could hide in a fist, atlases, fairy tales, manifestos printed small enough to smuggle. The Soviet cases are the most telling — when printing was state-controlled, miniature books became a showcase craft, proof the system could do exquisite things at any scale.

The fact to take with you: a miniature book is not a novelty but a technical boast. Setting readable type at two millimetres tests paper, ink, eyesight and patience at once, and binding it so the spine still opens flat is watchmaker's work. Hunt the tiniest book in the building — the labels argue over which currently holds the record — then check which country sent the newest arrival. It still grows.

Give it twenty minutes. Hours are small-museum hours, typically around 11:00 to 17:00 and often closed one weekday like Monday, so check before counting on it, with a step or two at the entrance. Then walk north-east about four hundred metres through the lanes toward the old walls and exit through the great double gate.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry, by the founder's principle. Verify opening days at the door — small museums keep small hours.
stops.openingHours: Typically open late morning to late afternoon, roughly 11:00 to 17:00, and usually closed one weekday (often Monday). Small museum, shifting hours — check before counting on it.
stops.accessibility: Small interior with tight display rooms; mostly level but cramped. The entrance has a step or two.
stops.insiderTip: Ask to use a magnifying glass and hunt the tiniest book in the building — then check the case labels for which country sent the newest arrival. The collection spans more than seventy countries.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the museum and walk north-east through the lanes for about four hundred metres toward the old walls. Exit the Old City through the great double gate in the fortifications — the Shamakhi Gate, our next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Stanislav Kozlovskiy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Shamakhi Gate (Gosha Gala)
stops.narration:
You are walking out of the Middle Ages through a double arch. This is the Shamakhi Gate — Gosha Gala in Azerbaijani, meaning Double Gate — the main northern exit of the Old City walls, named for the road that once ran to the old capital of Shamakhi. Two round bastions, one passage between them. Walk through slowly; you cross eight centuries in ten steps.

The walls are the lesson. Baku's Old City, called Icherisheher, the Inner City, was a fortress port, and these limestone ramparts were built and rebuilt between roughly the 12th and 19th centuries as Persians, Ottomans, Russians and local khans took turns ruling or besieging it. Russia finally took Baku in 1806, and under the Tsars the walls lost their military job: gates were widened, ditches filled, and the city spilled outward toward the oil fields. What saved them is the oldest preservation trick — they became picturesque just as they became useless.

Notice the stone under the arch: pale Absheron limestone, quarried from this very peninsula, soft when cut and hardening in air. Every empire here built in the same rock, which is why 12th-century towers and 19th-century mansions match. Late afternoon light hits the outer face dead-on, so turn around outside and photograph the gate looking back in — the twin towers frame the lanes perfectly.

No ticket here; it is a passage, open at all hours, level under the arch though surrounding pavements are uneven. Next is about two hundred metres north, toward water and café chatter. Follow your ears: Fountain Square opens ahead, and the fountains in the middle are the meeting point.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open fortifications, no ticket. It is a passage, not a site — walk through freely.
stops.accessibility: Level passage through the arch. The surrounding pavements are uneven in places.
stops.insiderTip: Photograph the gate from outside looking back in: the twin towers frame the Old City lanes perfectly, and late afternoon light hits the stone face-on.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north out of the gate for about two hundred metres toward the sound of water and café chatter. Fountain Square opens up in front of you — head for the fountains in the middle.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Самый древний, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Fountain Square
stops.narration:
Step out of the lanes and the city gets loud and Soviet. Fountain Square is Baku's living room — fountains, plane trees, café tables — laid out in Soviet times as a showcase downtown, when Azerbaijan was a republic of the USSR and Baku its oil capital. In a windy city on a salty sea, running fresh water in public was a statement that the state could provide.

Read the square like a timeline. On one side the Literature Museum carries statues of Azerbaijani poets on its facade — find Nizami, the 12th-century epic poet it is named for, whose lovers Layla and Majnun are the Romeo and Juliet of the Persian-speaking world. Around you sit 19th-century oil-boom facades, Soviet blocks and glass malls shoulder to shoulder. Nobody demolished anybody; Baku just builds the next era next door.

What you are really seeing is leisure as politics. Under the Soviets this was the evening promenade, the place to be seen; today it is the same, except the menus are longer and the square itself is free — you only pay café prices for what you sit down to eat or drink. Students, families, Gulf tourists, old men over backgammon: secular Azerbaijan, a Muslim-majority country where religion is mostly private, does its social life right here.

Take twenty minutes; the square is fully level and step-free, liveliest late afternoon into the night, best when the fountains are lit. Then walk south about fifteen minutes downhill toward the bay to the funicular lower station — the funicular, a small cable-hauled railway car that climbs the steep hill, costs about 1 manat each way, so keep coins or small notes. If it is closed for maintenance, take a taxi up instead.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free square. Cafés are at normal Baku prices. The funicular ride up next costs about 1 ₼ each way — carry coins or small notes.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Liveliest from late afternoon into the night.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free throughout. Benches everywhere.
stops.insiderTip: The Literature Museum facade statues read like a hall of fame of Azerbaijani poetry — find Nizami, the 12th-century epic poet the museum is named for. Evening, when the fountains are lit, is the square at its best.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south from the square for about fifteen minutes, downhill through the streets toward the bay, to the funicular lower station. Buy a ticket (about 1 ₼) and ride the little car to the top. If the funicular is closed for maintenance, take a taxi to Highland Park instead — do not attempt the steep road on foot in the heat.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Highland Park Viewpoint
stops.narration:
Hold your hat — Baku means City of Winds, and up here you learn why. You have ridden the funicular, the little Soviet-era cable-hauled railway car that climbs this otherwise punishing hill for about 1 manat each way, and stepped onto the Highland Park terrace over the bay. Below you the Caspian curves in a silver sickle, the Old City a honey-coloured knot, the boulevard a string of lights.

Read the panorama like a geologist. The bay is a perfect natural harbour, which is why people have lived here for millennia. The pale stone below is Absheron limestone, soft enough to carve and full of oil and gas — the rock that built the Old City also funded the glass towers. And that dark blue water is not a sea at all but the Caspian, the world's largest enclosed lake, with no outlet to any ocean. Its level rises and falls by metres across decades, which is why the Maiden Tower you stood in an hour ago once had waves at its foot and now sits hundreds of metres inland.

Give it twenty minutes. The twenty minutes before sunset are the show: the Old City glows gold, the bay turns silver, then the Flame Towers beside you switch on their LED skins. The terrace is open at all hours; the funicular typically runs roughly 10:00 to late evening but closes in maintenance spells, so check locally. The cars and main terrace are manageable, but ridge paths slope and the wind gusts — take it slow.

When ready, walk south along the ridge about two hundred metres, past the Flame Towers, toward the glowing graves around the eternal flame. That is Martyrs' Alley. Go quietly.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free viewpoint. The funicular up costs about 1 ₼ each way; verify it is running before walking to the lower station.
stops.openingHours: Terrace open access at all times. The funicular typically runs roughly 10:00 to late evening but closes for maintenance spells — check locally.
stops.accessibility: The funicular cars and the main terrace are step-manageable, but the park paths slope and gusty wind can unbalance. Take it slow on the ridge path.
stops.insiderTip: The twenty minutes before sunset are magic: the Old City glows honey-gold and the bay turns silver. After dark, stay a few minutes more — the Flame Towers' LED show starts and the boulevard lights string the whole bay.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south along the ridge path for about two hundred metres, past the Flame Towers, to the rows of glowing graves around the eternal flame. That is Martyrs' Alley — please go quietly.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Martyrs' Alley
stops.narration:
Lower your voice. You are entering Martyrs' Alley, and the mood is deliberately different from everywhere else on this walk. Rows of glowing graves face the bay, each with a portrait plaque, and an eternal flame burns at the end. People come here to mourn, not to sightsee. Treat it as they do.

The dead come from two wounds. In January 1990, as the Soviet Union collapsed, Soviet troops entered Baku and killed well over a hundred civilians in what Azerbaijanis remember as Black January — the funerals filled this hillside and gave the alley its name. Later graves hold soldiers killed in the Karabakh wars — Karabakh being the mountainous region contested between Christian Armenia and Muslim-majority Azerbaijan, fought over in the 1990s, retaken by Azerbaijan in the 2020 war and the 2023 offensive, after which around 100,000 Armenians fled. That is one sentence of a tragedy both peoples mourn; this hillside holds one people's grief. Remember the other exists.

Read a few plaques — ages, professions, families — and the monument stops being stone and starts being neighbours. That is the intended effect: the flame, the geometry, the graves facing the sea. Weddings lay flowers here, presidents lay wreaths, schoolchildren learn the names.

Stay as long as you like; it is free, open at all hours, the flame burning through the night, and the main avenue is level and step-free. Photographs are permitted but keep them quiet and distant, never posed. Then take the stairs and paths down the east side of the hill about ten minutes toward the water, to the rolled-carpet building on the promenade. That is where this walk ends.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free memorial, open to all. It is a place of mourning — treat it as one.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Visit in daylight or early evening; the flame burns through the night.
stops.accessibility: Level avenue along the ridge, step-free in the main memorial area. The descent stairs to the boulevard have many steps — take the path slowly.
stops.insiderTip: Read a few of the portrait plaques as you walk — ages, professions, families. The stones stop being a monument and start being neighbours. Then look up: the eternal flame with the bay behind it is the shot.
stops.nextStopDirections: Take the stairs and paths down the east side of the hill toward the water for about ten minutes, emerging on the seafront promenade by the rolled-carpet building. That is the Carpet Museum end of Baku Boulevard — our final stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: shankar s., CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Baku Boulevard
stops.narration:
You are down at the water, where Baku exhales. The boulevard — locals call it the Bulvar — runs for miles along the Caspian: joggers, wedding photographers, old men with backgammon boards. Turn around. The Flame Towers stand on the ridge behind you, and after dark they switch on their LED skins and burn blue and orange over the bay. Not subtle, and not trying to be.

Look along the waterfront for the other landmark: a huge building shaped like a rolled carpet, one end curled over. That is the Carpet Museum, and the joke writes itself until you go inside. Carpet-weaving here is not décor but language — each region knots its own patterns, colours and protective symbols, and for centuries a girl's dowry included carpets she wove herself. Oil money paid for the rolled-carpet shell; the knowledge inside is village knowledge, grandmother knowledge.

That split is the whole city. The boulevard began as a modest promenade a century ago, and Soviet and post-Soviet engineers kept pushing it further into the Caspian on reclaimed ground. What pays for all this is oil and gas — offshore Caspian fields fund the towers, the museum, the fountains, the paving under your feet. Supporters call it renewal; critics ask who shares the wealth and at what price in freedoms. Both are visible from where you stand.

So walk. The promenade is free but vendors, cafés, boat rides and museums charge separately. Wander five minutes to the canals of Little Venice, get tea, and look back after full dark for the LED flame show. You began at a 12th-century tower nobody can explain and end at three 21st-century towers nobody can miss. That is Baku's argument with itself, and you just walked through it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free promenade. Vendors, cafés, boat rides and the museums along it charge separately.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best at sunset and into the evening; the promenade stays lively late.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide, paved promenade — the most accessible stop on the tour. Benches throughout.
stops.insiderTip: Walk five minutes further along to Little Venice for the canals and bridges, and look back at the Flame Towers after full dark — the LED flame show is the city's goodnight.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Stroll either direction along the promenade — cafés, tea vendors, and taxis line the boulevard. The city centre and Fountain Square are a short taxi or a twenty-minute stroll back north.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Antoloji, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
